subject: Trying to interpret lp__ for super-simple model

messages.author: 4e78013477145d7d
messages.subject: Trying to interpret lp__ for super-simple model
parts:
I'm trying to intepret lp__ for a super-simple model:

normal_code <- '

data {
  int <lower=0> n;
  real x[n];
}

parameters {
  real mu;
}

model {
  x ~ normal(mu, 1);
}

'

But when I pass n=2, x=c(-1,1), I get lp__ = -1.489. This makes no sense to me.

As I understand things, the Bayesian probability of mu should be proportional to exp( -1 - mu^2). Integrate wrt mu, and we get exp(-1) * sqrt(pi).
Dividing, the posterior should be exp(-mu^2) / sqrt(pi), no? And at mu near 0, that would have lp ~ -0.57, no?

What am I doing wrong here?

messages.author: 0839befa8a8b7d53
messages.subject: Re: Trying to interpret lp__ for super-simple model
parts:
I believe the built-in distributions are smart enough to drop constants from the lp__ calculations. There's some discussion of this on page 115 of the manual (1.3.0).

That's my guess as to what is going on: the sqrt(pi) is not a function of a parameter (or transformed parameter yadda yadda), so it isn't added to lp__. If I'm right, if you do the updating manually with something like:

lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log( x , mu , 1 );

then the constant will be included and your back-of-envelop calculation will prove accurate.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Trying to interpret lp__ for super-simple model
parts: We drop all the constant terms. So when you write

model {
x ~ normal(mu, 1);
}

with x a data vector and mu a parameter and sigma=1, you get this
for the log probability up to an additive constant:

SUM_n - 0.5 * (x[n] - mu)^2

which because sigma = 1, reduces to

-0.5 * SUM_n (x[n] - mu)^2

The - log sigma^2 term is ignored, as is the sqrt(2 pi) and
sigma drops out of the denominator because it's a constant 1.
> As I understand things, the Bayesian probability

The posterior p(mu|y) is proportional to p(y|mu) * p(mu). And
because you have an improper uniform prior on mu, that works out
to be proportional to p(y|mu).

> of mu should be proportional to exp( -1 - mu^2). Integrate wrt
> mu, and we get exp(-1) * sqrt(pi).

I don't see why you want to integrate here. To get the posterior
expectation, which is what should be reported by the mean of mu in
the output?

As to where the -1.49 comes from, it depends on what mu is,
and that will vary across samples. Your example works out to:

- 0.5 * ((1 - mu)^2 + (-1 - mu)^2)

because you have x = [-1 1].

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Trying to interpret lp__ for super-simple model
parts:
On 8/20/13 4:45 PM, John Tillinghast wrote:
> Right now I'm not even thinking of model comparison. I am comparing STAN with some other ways of calculating integrals.

Stan's only really set up to give you integrals in the
form of posterior expectations.

E[f(theta)|y]

where f is an arbitrary function of the parameters theta
and the density of theta is the posterior p(theta|y).

> So the actual value of lp__ matters.
>
> The model and data are supposed to be ultra-trivial: two data points (-1 and 1). One parameter (mu, the mean of a normal
> distribution with sd=1).
>
> I believe the posterior density here is exp(- 0.5 * sum((x-mu)^2)) / Integral (same thing for mu from -inf to inf).
>
> Is it really something else?

Our messages saying the same thing crossed. But it is done
on the log scale. So we calculate the expectation of

- 0.5 * sum((x-mu)^2)

- Bob
